Why I am learning robotics

The most impressive robots of the last decade stayed in videos because they could not generalize. Language models changed that, and robotics now looks like language models in 2019.

September 28, 202620 min readUpdated October 27, 2026

roboticsindustry

1. The demo and the deployment

A backflip in 2017, a million robots without legs

In 2017 Boston Dynamics showed Atlas doing a backflip. A year later it was jumping over obstacles. Watching those clips, you could believe humanoids in your kitchen were a few years away.

Spot, the dog-shaped robot from the same company, went on sale in 2020 for $74,500, and more than 1,500 are with customers. Amazon says it runs 1,000,000 robots, and nearly all of them roll or stay bolted in place. (These counts come from different reports, so read them as orders of magnitude.)

Why didn't the backflip turn into a robot that does chores? You can plan a backflip ahead of time, but what if the robot starts tipping halfway through the jump? Atlas used a physics model of its own body to keep predicting what would happen next, and an optimizer to pick the forces to apply. That's model predictive control. Engineers designed a library of behavior templates offline, and the controller adapted them to the terrain as it went. It's beautiful engineering, and it means every new behavior needs a team of specialists to build it. The company also changed owners three times in eight years (Google in 2013, SoftBank in 2017, Hyundai in 2021), which I read as a sign that spectacular behaviors were hard to turn into a business.

Let's put a bag of groceries away in a kitchen the robot has never seen. The cereal brand is unfamiliar. The evening light is dim and yellow. The counter is taller than in the lab, and a mug blocks the milk's spot. You would barely notice any of this. Now suppose the mug blocks the path the robot's planner picked. Does the robot move it, go around it, or stop? With hand-engineered control, someone has to build a way to handle that.

Keeping a skill working when the object, the lighting, the surface height or the clutter changes, without anyone programming those cases, is what we call generalization. Hand-engineered control is bad at it. Learned policies have recently gotten a lot better at it, and that change is why I'm learning robotics now.

First, check the body

When a robot fails at the groceries, the hardware is the first suspect. Maybe the fingers are too clumsy, or the arm is too weak. Try teleoperation: a human drives the robot through a controller, using its motors and cameras. If a person can put the groceries away through the robot, the body is good enough for that task. If the robot then fails on its own, the missing piece is the policy, the program that turns what the robot sees into what it does next.

Run it on recent systems and the answer keeps pointing at the policy. In 2023, ACT used ALOHA, a pair of inexpensive and imprecise arms, to thread cable ties and insert batteries, with about 50 demonstrations per task. In 2024, Mobile ALOHA put the setup on wheels and learned to sauté shrimp, store a heavy pot and call an elevator, again from 50 demonstrations per task. Below, a person operates the robot through a three-course meal; alongside, the robot does housekeeping on its own. To me, the teleoperated meal is the interesting part: the body can already do all that. Getting it to choose those movements on its own is the bigger gap.

The hardware also got cheap. A Unitree G1 humanoid starts at $13,500, and the parts for an SO-101 arm cost a bit over $100. Hands are fragile, cables wear out, and batteries run down, and a robot that breaks every day is useless however smart its policy is.

Hardware endurance: why hands are hard

Most dexterous hands keep fingers light by putting motors in the forearm and pulling with tendons. Tendons can only pull, so every joint needs an opposing tendon or a spring, and routing them through the wrist adds friction, wear and tension to manage. Motors inside the fingers avoid the tendons but put mass and heat at the end of the arm. The Shadow hand uses 20 forearm motors with paired tendons. In August 2026, Figure's founder criticized an early tendon-hand design; that's his judgment, not reliability data. I'd want replaceable fingers, accessible cables, and repairs that don't mean rebuilding the arm.

Two ways to write the grocery program

Write the grocery program by hand and you get four stages. Perception finds the cereal box in the camera image. State estimation works out where the box and the arm are in space. Planning picks a path for the hand, and control turns that path into motor commands. An engineer tunes each stage; Atlas's controller excels at the last two. When the unseen cereal box shows up, some stage breaks and someone has to fix it.

The learned recipe replaces much of that pipeline with one network. Camera images, the instruction “put the groceries away” and the robot's joint angles go in, and the next action comes out. You collect demonstrations, usually by teleoperation, and train the network to imitate them. How much of the pipeline gets replaced varies from system to system.

One layer stays underneath. The policy outputs action commands. Commands for hand position and rotation must first be converted into joint targets, which feedback controllers track. Gravity pulls the arm down, friction resists the joints and the servos respond late, so the arm lands a little off target. That's the layer I'm studying in my SO-101 controller series, where I compare controllers (no winner yet). If joints and motors are new to you, start with from joint angles to a moving arm.

In February 2025, Figure showed Helix: two humanoids sharing one model, putting away groceries that included objects the company says were absent from training. In August, Boston Dynamics and TRI showed a newer generation of Atlas running one behavior model for legs and hands, learned from demonstrations. It ties rope, spreads a tablecloth, stacks blocks, and recovers when someone moves the box it's working on. Both are company demos.

The robot's brain started as a language model

The learned policy grew out of familiar language models:

ModelInputOutput
LLM (large language model)texttext, trained to predict the next piece of text
VLM (vision-language model)images and texttext
VLA (vision-language-action model)camera images, an instruction and the robot's joint stateactions

The usual way to build a VLA is to take a pretrained VLM and keep training it on robot data. That order matters for our groceries. From internet images and text, the VLM already knows what a cereal box looks like and what “put away” means, so the robot data only has to teach it how to move. RT-2 tested this in 2023 on objects, backgrounds and environments the robot had never seen, and success went from 32% with the earlier RT-1 to 62%.

Look at OpenVLA. Two image encoders, DinoV2 and SigLIP, turn the camera frame into features. But Llama 2, a 7-billion-parameter language model, expects text tokens, not the encoders' output. A small neural network converts that output into vectors Llama 2 can read alongside the instruction; this converter is the MLP projector in the diagram. We then convert Llama 2's output tokens back into seven numbers: three for how far to move the hand, three for how much to rotate it, and one for the gripper. That's one nudge toward the cereal box. The next frame comes in, and it does it again.

“Put the groceries away” is also a long instruction. Gemini Robotics 1.5 adds a reasoning model on top that splits a broad instruction into steps (open the fridge, pick up the milk) and hands each step to a VLA.

Nobody wrote the action data down

Language models got a gift: the internet was already full of text. Robots get no such gift. Records of robot observations, commands and contact mostly need deliberate collection, often by teleoperation. Our grocery policy needs lots of varied kitchens, our robot's body, measured commands and contact information, plus unseen kitchens for evaluation.

Three sources cover each other's weaknesses:

SourceWhat you getWhat it costs
TeleoperationCamera images paired with the executed commands and the measured motion: direct action labelsOperator time, scene resets, and real effort to get enough variety
SimulationRepeatable trials, known state, many experiments in parallelContact, friction, deformable objects and sensors behave differently in reality
Egocentric human videoFirst-person video, often head-mounted with hands visible, across many people, tasks, objects and placesNo measured motion or contact, and a human body instead of a robot

In 2023, Open X-Embodiment tried pooling experience across different bodies: about a million recorded attempts from 22 robot types. Could something learned on one arm help another? DROID kept the robot setup the same and changed its surroundings: 76,000 teleoperated attempts across 564 scenes in homes, offices and labs.

Human video is exciting: people already put groceries away every day. The hard part is moving the skill from a human hand to a robot hand. EgoScale (February 2026) does it in three stages, shown on the board. The middle stage uses matched data from a head camera, wrist cameras and tracked gloves, so every frame comes with the hand motion attached. On a robot hand with 22 degrees of freedom, they report a 54% improvement in average success over no pretraining.

Could you just mix human video into robot training and let the model figure out the connection? Kareer and colleagues at Physical Intelligence tried this in 2025 with their robot policy π0.5. They added 3 to 5 hours of head-camera video per task, without a separate step to match human movements to robot movements. To see what happened inside, they used t-SNE, which squashes the model's high-dimensional internal vectors down to 2D so you can look at them. Without robot pretraining, human and robot examples sit in separate clusters. With more diverse robot pretraining, the clusters overlap, as if the model had learned one description of the task for both bodies. On scenes that appeared only in the human video, performance nearly doubled.

In August 2026 Figure launched Index, a paid app for recording everyday activities, and reports more than 16,000,000 videos and 44,000 weekly users. In September it reported 56% task success in 30 homes the robot had never seen, against 9% without Index pretraining. A gap remains no matter how much video you collect: a human hand is not a robot hand.

Is this robotics' GPT-2 moment?

Compare the two fields:

YearLanguage modelsRobot learning
2017Transformer 
2018GPT-1, BERT 
2019GPT-2 
2020Scaling laws, GPT-3 
2022InstructGPT, ChatGPTSayCan, RT-1
2023 ACT, RT-2, Open X-Embodiment
2024 π0
2025 Helix, π0.5, Atlas behavior model
2026 Figure Index

My guess is that robotics in 2026 looks like language models around GPT-2 in 2019. GPT-2 showed that a bigger model trained on more data generalized better, and around the same period companies like Scale, Labelbox and Snorkel AI built an industry around producing data. Robotics has the same move now: people deliberately collecting data at scale, and investors starting to fund it. We might be closer to 2017, before scaling had shown much of anything, and I can't tell which from here.

EgoScale supplies the best scaling evidence I know of. They pretrained on 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 10,000 and 20,000 hours of human video. As they added video, the model's prediction error on data held aside for evaluation kept falling, roughly in a straight line against the logarithm of the hours: each doubling of video bought a similar drop in error. With the smaller datasets, the model learned the training examples better than it learned to handle new ones. Average task completion went from 0.30 at 1,000 hours to 0.71 at 20,000. That's one recipe on one robot with five data points: an early sign, far from a scaling law for robotics.

The analogy breaks in four places. Action data costs money to make, where text was lying around. The scaling evidence is still thin. A wrong word makes a bad sentence, while a wrong move breaks a glass. And errors compound over long tasks.

Say putting the groceries away takes 20 steps: open the fridge, pick up the milk, place it, and so on. Let p be the chance that a step succeeds once the robot has reached it, the same at every step, and assume a failed step ends the attempt. Then P(complete) = pn = 0.9520 ≈ 36%. So with a 95% chance of succeeding at each next step, only about 36 attempts in 100 finish all 20. That's much worse than 95% sounds! Recovery is exactly what breaks this formula, which is why I care so much about Atlas putting the box back after someone moves it.

In simulation, LIBERO and RoboCasa let you compare policies on the same tasks. RoboCasa365 gives us 365 everyday tasks in simulated kitchens, and the leading RoboCasa result in September 2026 completed only 36.7% of the multi-step tasks held out for evaluation. On a real robot, every trial needs someone to reset the kitchen, and the light and the objects drift between trials. When I read a result, I ask: does it recover, how much did the scenes vary, how many trials were repeated, how often did a human help, how long did it run, and what did maintenance cost.

What self-driving already worked out

Self-driving is the one place where a learned robot already runs in the open world at scale. Waymo reports more than 270,000,000 fully autonomous miles through June 2026 and, against human drivers in the same cities, 82% fewer injury crashes and 95% fewer crashes with serious injury or worse. The matching method and error bars aren't in the summary.

They test in closed-loop simulation, where the other cars react to what the Waymo does, and an automated Critic reviews millions of real miles and tens of billions of simulated miles every week to dig out rare events. They also say real driverless operation, with real responsibility, was necessary. And their model also reports which objects it sees and how the roads connect, alongside the path it wants to drive. A separate onboard checker asks whether the car can physically follow that path and whether it obeys traffic rules. FieldAI describes a similar mix of learned models, physics-based reasoning and uncertainty estimates. For manipulation this is still open: how much do you learn end to end, and where do physics, structure, uncertainty and independent checks go?

The big difference is contact. A car's main job is to touch nothing. A grocery robot's main job is to touch things on purpose: grasp the milk, push the mug aside, squeeze the bread without crushing it, pour. Friction, slip and deformation make those contacts hard to predict, and they're exactly what simulators get wrong. So manipulation will need the same mix of simulation and real deployment, with contact as the hard part to transfer.

Before we push the mug, could we predict whether it will slide aside or tip over? That's what we'd like a world model to tell us. You give it what the robot sees now and a candidate action, and it predicts what happens next, as future pixels or as more abstract features. If the predictions are good, you can try actions in imagination before you commit, generate synthetic demonstrations, and test a policy before it touches a real kitchen. All of it depends on how faithful the predictions are.

The Waymo World Model, built on Genie 3, generates camera and lidar data conditioned on driving actions, scene layout or text, to cover extreme weather and strange objects on the road. DreamGen starts from one real robot-camera image, lets a robot-adapted video model imagine the rest of the task, then recovers the actions from the generated video with inverse dynamics (a model that looks at consecutive frames and infers the action between them). Seeded with teleoperation data from one pick-and-place task in one environment, it gave a humanoid 22 new behaviors. 1X's NEO (January 2026) runs this loop live: a voice or text request plus the current camera view go in, the model generates the future video, and inverse dynamics turns it into motion.

V-JEPA 2 takes the other route on the board. It predicts future features instead of pixels, so it never has to render every crumb on the counter. It learns first from more than 1,000,000 hours of video without action labels, then from under 62 hours of robot data, and uses its predictions to plan movements. AMI, associated with Yann LeCun, is pursuing this feature-prediction route.

Why cheaper task changes could move factories

The board shows 2024 robot density in manufacturing, with South Korea at 1,220 robots per 10,000 employees and the United States at 307. Today's factory robot lives in a cell built for one task, and every task change means paying someone to integrate and reprogram it. At high volume that cost spreads over a lot of parts. With small batches, fewer parts share the integration cost, making automation harder to justify and cheap manual labor more attractive.

Now move the grocery skill to a workbench: a robot that picks up a new task from a few dozen demonstrations in an afternoon. Task changes get cheap, small batches become worth automating, and the reason to send work to low-wage countries weakens. With an aging workforce in Europe and reshoring policies in place, that could make local manufacturing viable again. It happens only if the policies generalize and run reliably in production.

In January 2026 Boston Dynamics announced the production Atlas, a partnership with Google DeepMind on Gemini, and a Hyundai factory with an announced capacity of 30,000 robots a year. Hyundai plans to start with parts sequencing in its car plants.

Embodiment choice: does it need to look human?

Doors, shelves, tools and workstations were all built for human bodies, which is the case for a humanoid. Specialized wheels and arms already do warehouse work at huge scale. Figure 02 moved more than 90,000 components in about 1,250 operating hours at BMW Spartanburg, and Agility's Digit moved more than 100,000 totes at a GXO facility. Both are defined, repetitive jobs, and the reports don't tell you about profit or how much human help was involved. I'd compare bodies on the whole job: task success, human help, uptime and maintenance cost. Looking human earns nothing by itself.

How I'm learning it

Robotics is also unusually easy to start right now. The papers are open, the simulators are accessible, an arm costs about $100 in parts, and coding agents write experiment code fast. In EmbodiedSWE, the best agent solved about 82% of 28 simulated tasks, while a real lamp-disassembly policy fine-tuned on 500 of its generated demonstrations succeeded in 2 of 10 trials. The benchmark and the lamp test use different task sets, so the two numbers don't tell us what caused the gap, and ten trials is a small sample. I'd want to see the agent working on a real object.

Coding agents as robot researchers

EmbodiedSWE has a coding agent write, run and revise solutions to simulated tasks, then uses the verified programs to generate demonstrations. Agent as Policy keeps the coding agent inside the real-robot control loop. On three block tasks it scored 5/5, 5/5 and 4/5, but each run took 21 to 35 minutes, which is far too slow for a kitchen.

That speed makes it easy to explore forever, hand the design to the agent, and end up with no concrete result and no understanding. So I keep four jobs for myself: predict what an experiment will show before I run it, choose which experiment to run, explain each failure, and write it up clearly enough that you can follow it. (Jacob Rothschild's post pushed me toward this.)

The next time you see a robot video, ask: Could a teleoperator do it, so is the body enough? Would it still work with the unseen cereal box in the dim kitchen? And when a step goes wrong, can it recover and finish the job without someone helping? A cheap arm lets us try these experiments ourselves. That's why I'm learning robotics.
